edge.title: The tingle in the water
edge.anchor: Two foreigners died of suspected electrocution in the swimming pool of a five-star hotel in Bengaluru (NDTV, Deccan Herald, The Hindu).
edge.setup: You are in a hotel or apartment pool, or standing in wet shoes beside it, and you feel a faint tingle, buzz or prickle on your skin. It is mild, nobody else has said anything, and the pool looks perfectly clean and expensive. It is easy to put down to cold water or your imagination.
edge.tell: A tingle, buzz or shock while wet. Treat it as electricity until proven otherwise.
move: Get out of the water at once and tell the others to get out. Do not wait to be sure.
If someone is unresponsive in the water, do not jump in after them, because you can become the next casualty. Shout for staff, ask for the power to be switched off and call 112.
Report it to the front desk or society office, and do not go back in until someone qualified has checked it.
At home, keep wet hands and feet away from switches, extension boards and water heaters, and replace any cracked or exposed wiring.
edge.why: Water conducts electricity, and a wet body conducts it far better than dry skin. A pool is a metal-and-wire environment (lights, pumps, ladders) sitting in water, so a small fault can put current where people are. The tingle is the early, survivable warning; the only cheap defence is to act on it before it becomes a larger current. A premium look says nothing about the wiring behind it.
edge.variants: Same shape: a mild shock from a bathroom geyser or tap, a wet-floor kitchen appliance that buzzes, a metal lamp post or hoarding that tingles in the rain.

lens.name: Costly signals
lens.one_line: A signal is only trustworthy if it is expensive for a liar to fake.
lens.detail: We rely on cheap markers of trust: a local phone number, a logo, a polished video, a confident tone. They work only while faking them costs more than the fraud earns. When technology makes a marker cheap to copy, it stops carrying information, and you must switch to something the faker cannot produce cheaply.
elsewhere: A letterhead or PDF 'offer letter' versus a verified company email domain.
A five-star review count versus a reviewer with a long, varied history.
A flat shown in a video versus a key that turns in the lock.
lens.test: What would this signal cost a liar to fake? If almost nothing, treat it as no evidence.
lens.today: The Times of India asks, after the hotel pool deaths, whether safety is assured at a five-star property. A star rating and a polished lobby are cheap to display and say little about the wiring behind the pool. Judge a place by something a careless operator could not easily fake, such as a visible safety certificate you can ask to see, or by how staff react when you report a problem.

moved.so_what: If you drop a token or card, ask station staff to retrieve it, because one incident can cost every rider about 20 minutes. Keep a small buffer on metro-dependent trips.
